uncited: This family addresses the problem of applying spatial transformations (rigid body motion, scaling, deformation) to Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDFs) during ray marching or voxel processing.
It enables the rendering of animated, deforming, or dynamically positioned geometry without recomputing the underlying distance field data structures from scratch.

It differs from static SDF definitions by introducing time-varying coordinate mappings, and from explicit mesh transformation by operating directly on the implicit field representation (or its voxel approximation) to preserve the analytical or volumetric nature of the distance query.
All methods in this family rely on the principle of coordinate space transformation.

The core mechanism involves mapping a query point from the rendering space (world space or camera space) into the local space of the primitive or the reference frame of the data before evaluating the distance function or sampling the voxel grid.
For rigid transformations, the mapping is defined by a transformation matrix $M$.
For non-rigid or temporal transformations (such as motion compensation in TSDF compression), the mapping is often estimated per-block or per-voxel.
The goal is to predict the current state $s_t$ from a previous state $s_{t-1}$ using an estimated rigid transform $(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})$.
Scaling introduces a change in the metric of the distance field.
For uniform scaling by factor $s$, the distance value must be scaled to preserve the Euclidean distance property: $f'(\mathbf{p}) = s \cdot f(\mathbf{p}/s)$ [S35, unofficial].
An algorithm for scaling voxel grids that avoids floating-point accumulation errors by using incremental updates.
- If scaling factors are greater than 1, forward scaling may produce holes due to volume increase without voxel increase.
